title: Tips for Building Creator-led Brands
summary: Use these expert tips to build a creator-led brand, or to adapt creator-led strategies into a traditional DTC model.
body_markdown:
Creator-led brands are businesses helmed by influencers who have meaningful audiences across social channels like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, and are using that reach to build companies across categories like beauty, apparel, and food.


“I think this is one of the biggest movements right now in the creator space,” says[Alex Bushman](https://www.instagram.com/alexbushman/?hl=en) , founder and CEO of[Influencer Social Responsibility (ISR)™](https://www.influencersocialresponsibility.com/) , an agency that partners with creators and brands on social impact campaigns. Audiences are already buying based on what creators share. According to a[2026 Sprout Social survey](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/press/new-research-finds-influencer-reach-is-no-longer-tied-to-follower-count/) , 81% of Gen Z consumers made a purchase based on an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.


In this guide, Alex walks through why the creator-led model is gaining traction, tips for creators looking to build their own business, and what traditional brands can learn from creator-led brands.


## What are creator-led brands?


Creator-led brands are businesses founded by content creators who turn an existing audience or a trusted voice into a commercial brand. In these businesses, creators either found or play a central role in the company’s public identity, product development, distribution, and content, as opposed to simply functioning as spokespersons.


Examples include women’s apparel brand[Dairy Boy](https://dairyboy.com/) , founded by lifestyle creator Paige Paul, skincare brand[Reale Actives](http://realeactives.com/) from beauty and fashion creator Alix Earle, and home décor brand[Lone Fox](https://lonefox.com/) by DIY creator Drew Scott.


Unlike traditional[direct-to-consumer (DTC)](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/direct-to-consumer) brands, creator-led brands build on an audience’s existing trust rather than relying primarily on paid acquisition. “They already have the audience, trust, and content engine to be putting these brands out there,” says Alex. These brands benefit from the personal connection creators have established with followers across social media platforms.

## Tips for building a creator-led brand


- Create products around your audience’s preferencesv
- Double down on what makes you unique
- Let your personal brand focus your product line


Read on for tips from Alex and other influencer-founders on how creators can build their own brands:


### Create products around your audience’s preferences


One of the main benefits of launching a brand as a creator is the built-in audience. “It used to be that you would build a product and then build the community,” Alex says. “Now it’s build the community and then launch the product.” Creators can use their relationship with their audience to better understand[consumer behavior](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/consumer-behavior-trends) and create products that specifically cater to their followers.


Drew Scott built his brand[Lone Fox](https://lonefox.com/) based on what he learned from his YouTube audience. His DIY home videos drew a million views in a couple of weeks, far more than his fashion content, so he launched a separate channel, Lone Fox, which now has more than 1.7 million subscribers. On an episode of *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/lone-fox-inventory-and-content-strategies-that-sell)* , he says reading comments showed him what viewers liked about his DIY projects. “I started noting those things down,” he says, and those notes guided the products he sells.


Other creator-founders ask their audiences directly, both by polling and scheduling short calls. On *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/set-active-inventory-management)* ,[Set Active](https://setactive.co/) Founder Lindsey Carter says she posts questions like “Do you like this color?” and “Do you like this style?” These prompts draw “thousands and thousands and thousands of votes.”[Sock Candy](https://sockcandy.com/) Founder Mary Gui says on *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/sock-candy-reddit-and-creative-marketing-tips)* that she interviewed customers one-on-one over Zoom and heard requests like a knee-length version of a sock style.


A[Shopify online store](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/index) gives you a destination where you can send followers when they’re ready to buy. With Shopify’s[social commerce channels](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/social-commerce/index) , you can sync products to your Instagram and Facebook shops, tag them in posts and stories, and promote products through videos.


### Double down on what makes you unique


As a creator, you likely already have a niche. When you turn it into a brand, lean into what sets you apart from others in your space.


Alex points to Dairy Boy founder Paige Paul as an example of a creator who has successfully differentiated her brand. “The influencer space, I think, is so New York City–focused, or LA-focused, and Paige flipped that on its head and was like, I actually really resonate with this slower, Americana lifestyle, like in a cottage with chickens roaming around,” Alex says. “She built a world that people want to be part of.”


Mary Gui leaned into a styling quirk that her followers already noticed. “My followers would always comment about my socks. So I started to realize this is something that people know me for that’s also unique. … I realized that there was a gap in the marketplace.” Because she was already styling socks with her outfits, which not many other creators were doing, Mary felt uniquely qualified to fill that gap.


### Let your personal brand focus your product line


Your personal brand as a creator can help you decide which products to launch and which ideas to skip. Before selling a product, ask whether it’s something your audience already associates with you.


Drew Scott originally stocked Lone Fox with contemporary home goods from wholesalers until he realized, “I’m selling all this stuff on my site, but I’m not using any of it.” The products were also easy to find elsewhere; he’d see the vase he was selling on Amazon. Meanwhile, he says, “people were loving the vintage I was using in my projects,” so he began selling mostly one-of-a-kind vintage pieces, which he sources himself. He credits that change with the brand’s sales more than doubling from 2024 to 2025.


Lone Fox draws on the refurbishing skills Drew’s audience follows him for. His team puts new shades on vintage lamps and reupholsters furniture to “rework and reimagine them” for modern living.


## What traditional brands can learn from creator-led brands


- Share the building of your brand
- Put a face to your brand name
- Choose your partners strategically


You don’t need a creator-founder or a large following to borrow from this playbook. Here are a few ideas you can apply to your business, inspired by creator-led brands:


### Share the building of your brand


“What creator-led brands do really well, I think, is show the entire process of building a brand,” says Alex. “Not just the finished product, not just the perfect final result, but the behind-the-scenes of building the brand, everything that goes wrong.”


She points to[Good Girl Snacks](https://goodgirlsnacks.com/) Cofounders Yasaman Bakhtiar and Leah Marcus as an example. “They’re two best friends who take you on every step of their journey. They talk about everything that went wrong; they talk about when they did their mailers and the pickle jars broke,” she says. To do this type of storytelling, Alex says to film as much as possible and not shy away from “the messy parts of building a business.”


Lindsey of Set Active echoes the same sentiment: “If you’re building a brand and you haven’t raised money yet, or you’re just about to start a raise, or you’re bootstrapping it, you have to show your consumer what you’re working on. They want the passion, they want the story to buy into, they want to root for the underdog,” she says.


### Put a face to your brand name


Consider creating brand content around people rather than just your product. “In this day and age, especially with AI, people are connecting to real human stories,” says Alex. “And when you know why a person is starting the brand, it makes everything more meaningful.”


Highlighting the humans behind the brand can mean sharing your story as a founder or showing your employees in action. “Any sort of community or humanity that you could give the brand will perform really well,” says Alex. On *[Shopify Masters](https://www.shopify.com/blog/hugz-creator-led-mental-health-brand)* ,[Hugz](https://givehugz.co/) Cofounder Lexi Hensler highlights the importance of a personal narrative: “You could have the most viral videos in the world, but if these people don’t know anything about you and your story and your mission, why are they going to buy what you’re selling?” For Hugz, which sells weighted stuffed animals, that means “having a founder presence” on social media. In her video posts, Lexi opens up about struggling with panic attacks as a teen and looking for something comforting to hold.


### Choose your partners strategically


Traditional brands can reach new audiences by[partnering with content creators](https://www.shopify.com/blog/content-creators) , but Alex recommends choosing them based on alignment rather than follower count. “I think the quality of followers is way more important now than quantity of followers,” she says, particularly if the goals are building trust and increasing sales.


Depending on the goals for your campaign, Alex says you might consider[micro-creators](https://www.shopify.com/blog/micro-influencer) over those with large followings, or work with a combination of influencer types. And, if you find the right influencer, she says, “there’s an opportunity to work with them in a bigger way down the line.”


Some creator partners even become investors. Alix Earle created content for soda brand[Poppi](https://www.drinkpoppi.com/) in exchange for equity rather than cash and also invested her own money in Poppi. These relationships could be a significant opportunity, Alex says, “especially if you’re a small business and looking to get more people on your cap table.” (A cap table is the list of people who own equity in your business.)


As you build your creator network, tools like[Shopify Collabs](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/collabs/merchants/online-store-page) can help you pinpoint the right creators for your brand and manage affiliate and creator partnerships.


## Creator-led brands FAQ


### What is a creator brand?


Creator-led brands are businesses founded or cofounded by creators who turn an existing audience or a trusted voice into a commercial brand. The creator plays a central role in the company’s public identity, product development, distribution, and content, tailoring them to suit their target audience.


### What are some popular influencer-led brands?


Examples of creator-led brands include the lifestyle brand[Dairy Boy](https://dairyboy.com/) , founded by Content Creator Paige Paul; skincare brand[Reale Actives](http://realeactives.com/) by Beauty and Fashion Creator Alix Earle; and DIY Creator Drew Scott’s home décor brand[Lone Fox](https://lonefox.com/) .


### Can I create my own brand?


Yes, if you’re a creator, use your audience’s feedback to help guide your business. If you’re a traditional entrepreneur, consider incorporating your own story into your business to highlight your authenticity and engender consumers’ trust. Regardless of your following, consider your mission statement and the “why?” behind your brand.
